authoring_note: All scenario stems and response options are original content written for this deliverable. They are informed by the public six-element, three-level structure and by the role-profile purposes, but do not reproduce Jisc wording.

deployment_model.selection_rule: For bdc-individual, use both universal scenarios for each element and boundary. For a specialised profile, use the role-specific 01 scenario as the primary scenario for each element and boundary and pair it with the universal 02 scenario for that same element and boundary.

scenarios.scenario_stem: A shared digital workspace is introduced for a recurring piece of work. Files, comments and deadlines are currently split across different places, and people keep using out-of-date versions.

response_options.text: Keep using personal or ad hoc workarounds around shared file spaces. They are familiar and feel quicker than changing the routine.
Create a consistent way of using shared file spaces, move current work into the shared workflow, and use the built-in features that make everyday work or study more dependable.
Do that, then add a short guide or review point so the use of core productivity apps becomes easier for other people to follow and improve.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates familiar workaround behaviour from independent control of a dependable workflow.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You switch between devices and locations during a normal week. A routine task becomes messy when the latest file is unclear and the meeting or submission details are buried in old messages.

response_options.text: Start again from whichever copy is easiest to find and ask other people to resend what you need.
Use synced storage, one dependable place for links and notes, and the recovery features in shared file spaces or core productivity apps to get back to the current version.
Build a repeatable system across devices or locations, tidy permissions and backups, and make the recovery pattern easy to repeat next time.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates familiar workaround behaviour from independent control of a dependable workflow.

scenarios.scenario_stem: A small group asks you to improve a digital workflow that feels clumsy and unreliable. The current mix of tools technically works, but people regularly miss steps and duplicate effort.

response_options.text: Show colleagues the tips that work for you personally and leave uptake optional.
Review the workflow end to end, simplify how calendar and task tools and shared file spaces are used, create a workable standard, and adjust it with feedback.
Introduce a more advanced platform first because extra features should solve the friction, even if the workflow itself stays unclear.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates strong personal use from the ability to review, simplify and improve digital workflow choices for others.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You are asked to recommend whether to adopt a new digital tool for a recurring task. The current approach is workable, but there is pressure to modernise quickly.

response_options.text: Keep the current mix of tools and add written tips so people can work around the friction themselves.
Compare the options against access, interoperability, privacy, support burden and likely adoption, then recommend the choice that improves the overall workflow.
Choose the platform with the most features because advanced users will appreciate the extra power.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates strong personal use from the ability to review, simplify and improve digital workflow choices for others.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You need to create a digital output for a real need, and there is an older example available. People expect something usable soon.

response_options.text: Copy the previous example, update the surface details and publish it quickly.
Start from the user need, adapt or build digital resources purposefully, and make specific choices about structure, format and access.
Do that, then test templates or prototypes with intended users and refine it so the solution is easier to reuse or adapt later.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates copying or cosmetic adjustment from purposeful design around a genuine user need.

scenarios.scenario_stem: A repeated manual task is wasting time and causing avoidable mistakes. You have access to common digital tools that could change how the work is done.

response_options.text: Keep the manual workaround because it is familiar and avoids the risk of changing the process.
Use available tools to redesign the task so repeated steps are reduced and the output is clearer, easier to use and better aligned with the need.
Prototype the redesign, gather feedback from real users and turn the result into a documented pattern that could be reused.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates copying or cosmetic adjustment from purposeful design around a genuine user need.

scenarios.scenario_stem: A successful one-off digital solution now needs to serve a wider group. Colleagues want to know how to take it further.

response_options.text: Produce a polished one-off version for the immediate case, even if nobody else could easily reuse it.
Co-design a reusable pattern around digital resources or templates or prototypes, document assumptions, test it with users and decide what to scale.
Copy the most fashionable format from elsewhere and assume it will transfer locally.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates effective one-off making from reusable, evaluated and evidence-led innovation.

scenarios.scenario_stem: People say they want innovation in this area, but the last few ideas looked impressive without solving the underlying problem.

response_options.text: Add more interactive or eye-catching features so the output looks more innovative.
Identify the real problem, run a measured experiment, evaluate what changed and then decide whether to scale, adapt or stop.
Choose the example that looks most successful elsewhere and copy it before checking local fit.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates effective one-off making from reusable, evaluated and evidence-led innovation.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You completed a piece of digital development activity that looked useful. The question is what happens next in your actual practice.

response_options.text: Save the materials from short courses and guides and return to them only if a similar problem appears again.
Choose one change to apply soon, use it in a real task, and note what worked and what still needs attention.
Plan the application, gather feedback or evidence of change from practice experiments, and share what you learned so others can benefit too.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates reactive exposure to learning from planned application and reflection in practice.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You need to pick up a new digital method quickly because a task now depends on it. There is plenty of guidance available, but little time.

response_options.text: Learn only what is needed to finish the immediate task, then move on.
Use a mix of guidance and practice on a real task until the new method works with reasonable independence.
Turn the learning into a small improvement cycle, comparing approaches and curating the most useful resources for future use.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates reactive exposure to learning from planned application and reflection in practice.

scenarios.scenario_stem: After you found an approach that works, colleagues ask for help. They vary in confidence and have different starting points.

response_options.text: Give a quick demo of the tool or method you prefer and let people take from it what they want.
Design a short learning sequence using short courses and guides or peer learning exchanges, include practice and reflection, and follow up on what people apply.
Share a long list of resources and treat access to them as enough support.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates informal advice-giving from structured development that helps other people change practice.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You have some responsibility for raising digital confidence in a small group. Enthusiasm is mixed and time is limited.

response_options.text: Run a one-off awareness session and treat attendance as the main sign of success.
Sequence support over time, provide examples and safe practice opportunities, and adapt the support from feedback and observed use.
Focus first on the enthusiasts and assume the rest will follow later once the benefits become obvious.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates informal advice-giving from structured development that helps other people change practice.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You need to prepare a brief or make a decision using digital sources. Several sources are easy to find and look convincing.

response_options.text: Use the sources or figures that look clear and professional if they broadly support the task.
Check who produced the evidence, how current and relevant it is, and whether the measures or definitions actually fit the question.
Compare the limits of several sources, combine searches and source collections or spreadsheets or dashboards where helpful, and explain confidence and gaps before deciding.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates convenient information use from deliberate evaluation and interpretation of evidence.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You are given a shared spreadsheet or dashboard and asked what the figures mean. The visual summary looks neat, but the underlying data is not yet clear.

response_options.text: Reuse the default summary or chart without checking how the figures were defined or cleaned.
Inspect fields, timeframes and missing data, then interpret the figures carefully against the actual question being asked.
Audit the assumptions, combine the figures with other relevant evidence and make the uncertainty explicit before drawing conclusions.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates convenient information use from deliberate evaluation and interpretation of evidence.

scenarios.scenario_stem: A group is leaning heavily on a confident evidence claim from a vendor, media source or stakeholder with a clear interest in the outcome.

response_options.text: Use the claim if it supports what the group already wants to do, while noting that every source has some bias.
Interrogate the provenance, method and incentives behind the evidence, then synthesize the strongest points and the limits for other people.
Reject the source entirely because it comes from an interested party, without weighing whether some parts are still informative.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates competent individual judgment from synthesis and communication of uncertainty for others.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You need to combine different kinds of evidence to advise on next steps. The evidence does not line up perfectly.

response_options.text: Choose the cleanest dataset and ignore harder-to-compare evidence because it will only complicate the message.
Synthesize the relevant quantitative and qualitative evidence, show where they converge or conflict and recommend action with stated confidence.
Wait until the evidence is complete and perfectly comparable before offering any interpretation.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates competent individual judgment from synthesis and communication of uncertainty for others.

scenarios.scenario_stem: A group is working online, but messages are scattered and decisions are easy to miss. People are starting to duplicate effort.

response_options.text: Use every available channel so nobody can say they missed the message.
Agree which channel does what, keep updates concise, and use shared spaces so current decisions and contributions are easier to find.
Do that, then build inclusive routines for participation, summarise decisions and adjust the pattern from how people actually engage.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates habitual participation from intentional coordination and channel design.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You need to collaborate with people who have different schedules, preferences or locations. The task requires both contribution and clarity.

response_options.text: Stick to the channel you know best and let other people adapt to it.
Choose tools and norms that fit the task, clarify response expectations and make asynchronous contribution easy where needed.
Facilitate across synchronous and asynchronous modes, remove participation barriers and monitor whether contributions are balanced.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates habitual participation from intentional coordination and channel design.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You are asked to coordinate digital collaboration on a shared project involving more than one team or group.

response_options.text: Create a lively chat space and rely on frequent updates to keep momentum high.
Design roles, channel purposes and decision points, and actively support balanced, respectful participation across the group.
Launch a new platform for the group and assume the community will organise itself around it.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates active contribution from facilitation of inclusive, purposeful collaboration.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You help run an online community or shared digital space where useful participation matters more than simple activity counts.

response_options.text: Keep communication highly formal so nothing becomes messy, even if participation drops.
Set expectations, nurture useful exchanges, manage conflict early and model respectful, accessible participation.
Post regular content yourself because a busy feed is the clearest sign that the community is healthy.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates active contribution from facilitation of inclusive, purposeful collaboration.

scenarios.scenario_stem: A recent near miss makes you realise that your digital presence, privacy or availability is less intentional than it should be.

response_options.text: Tighten the setting or habit that caused the latest problem and carry on otherwise unchanged.
Review your presence, privacy, availability and habits across contexts, then make changes that fit your role and risk level.
Do that, then turn the review into a deliberate, revisitable approach to boundaries, trust and sustainability that others could understand.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates reactive fixes from deliberate management of digital presence, boundaries and wellbeing.

scenarios.scenario_stem: Notifications, visibility and blurred expectations are starting to drain your attention. You need a healthier digital pattern.

response_options.text: Mute or reduce things temporarily whenever they become overwhelming.
Set sustainable boundaries for notifications, channels and availability, and manage your presence so it supports rather than drains your work.
Combine personal boundary-setting with a clear model for healthy digital practice that you can explain and revisit as contexts change.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates reactive fixes from deliberate management of digital presence, boundaries and wellbeing.

scenarios.scenario_stem: Other people ask for advice about digital conduct, boundaries or wellbeing because your own practice seems reliable.

response_options.text: Share the privacy settings and habits that work for you and assume they will fit most people.
Help shape shared norms around visibility, tone, safety, workload and care, while recognising different risks and needs.
Focus mainly on public polish and regular posting, since visible professionalism should reassure people.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates sound personal habits from the ability to influence wider digital norms and care.

scenarios.scenario_stem: You represent yourself or your organisation in digital spaces where credibility matters. Visibility has benefits, but so do boundaries and care.

response_options.text: Keep your own settings and boundaries in good order and assume that visible example is enough.
Balance visibility, authenticity, boundaries and care, and use your digital presence to reinforce trustworthy norms.
Avoid public or semi-public digital engagement wherever possible so that risk stays minimal.

scenarios.discrimination_notes: This scenario separates sound personal habits from the ability to influence wider digital norms and care.
